doc.title: Oscar Peterson interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Playing two pianos with Basie, the baseball bat and the eights
summary: The 'Satch and Josh' two-piano routine with Basie, the Paige-Gibson story, and Basie's timing in trading eights.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I laugh because you told the story on yourself, somewhere I heard you telling the story on the air, you were playing and you got into some stride at the piano, and you were playing and you said you couldn’t get out of it, it just came, it just happened, and you happened to look in the wings, and there was Basie going —

That’s right. He brought a baseball bat. We used to do this Satch and Josh thing, with the two pianos. And one night he came out on the stage and Norman said, “and on the two pianos we have Oscar Peterson and Bill Basie, would you welcome them?” I walked up from this end and Basie walked from the other. He had a baseball bat.

For those of you who don’t quite understand, I must explain. You see, Basie and Oscar did a thing together. And the Satch — they told this story about Satchell Paige and Josh Gibson who was the greatest hitter I guess in baseball at the time, Negro baseball. He told Satchell Paige he said, “My mother and father are coming to watch me play. And at some point, Satchell, would you please let me hit one?” You know.

He didn’t say okay, he just nodded, and said hmmm, all right, it’s like that. So now the game is on and Josh comes up, knocks the dust off his spikes and steps in, and looks at Satchell and Satchell shakes his head like this and — Shoooook — aspirin. Shoooook — aspirin. So probably the third time, this happened twice, the third time he came up, he say Josh knocked the dust off his cleats and looked at Satchell and [shakes head].

You can not hit it today. And so the idea was, Basie would look across at two pianos, and look at Oscar as if to say, “are you going to let me hit just one today? May I hit a key?” That was so, and you had to know the story.

He was beautiful. But you know he had a— he did so much with the piano in doing so little as many people think, but he did a lot. Because Basie could destroy you, whatever you’d play. We played, as you’d call them “eights” — challenges — eight bars for him, eight bars for me. And I’d play my eight bars, you know, and do my thing, and Basie would come up to his eight bars and he’d go like [brief scat] and wipe me out. You know, he had that ability, because his timing was impeccable. His choice of where to put what.
